title: Harmony and Voice Leading III: Embellishments, Motives, and Melodic Devices

guide.summary: Unit 6 covers embellishing tones (non-chord tones), motives and their transformations, and melodic devices composers use to create unity and variety.

sections.heading: Non-chord tones
sections.body: Passing tone: approached and left by step in the same direction, filling in a third (accented or unaccented). Neighbor tone: step away and back to the same chord tone (upper or lower). Suspension: a note held over from the previous chord (preparation), dissonant on a strong beat (suspension), resolving down by step (resolution); named by intervals above the bass: 4–3, 7–6, 9–8, and 2–3 in the bass. Retardation: like a suspension but resolving up. Appoggiatura: approached by leap, left by step (usually in the opposite direction), typically accented. Escape tone: approached by step, left by leap in the opposite direction. Anticipation: a note of the next chord arriving early. Pedal point: a sustained (often bass) note held against changing harmonies.

sections.heading: Motives and transformations
sections.body: A motive is a short, recognizable musical idea. Composers develop motives by repetition, sequence (repetition at a different pitch level), inversion (intervals turned upside down), retrograde (backward), augmentation (longer note values), diminution (shorter values), and fragmentation (using part of the motive). Real sequences preserve exact intervals; tonal sequences adjust to the key.

sections.heading: Melodic analysis
sections.body: Identify chord tones first, then classify each remaining note by how it is approached and left. Consider metric placement: accented dissonances (suspensions, appoggiaturas, accented passing tones) create expressive tension. In dictation and aural questions, listen for characteristic shapes: the step-step of passing tones, the step-back of neighbors, and the held-then-falling suspension.

sections.heading: Worked example: labeling non-chord tones
sections.body: To analyze a melody over chords, first circle the chord tones in each harmony. Then examine each remaining note: if it is approached and left by step in the same direction, it is a passing tone; by step and back, a neighbor; held over from the previous chord and resolved down by step, a suspension; approached by leap and left by step, an appoggiatura; approached by step and left by leap, an escape tone; arriving early as part of the next chord, an anticipation. Label suspensions by intervals above the bass, such as 4–3 or 7–6.

sections.heading: Melodic dictation strategies
sections.body: In melodic dictation, you hear a short melody several times. On the first hearing, listen for the overall shape, meter, and cadence. On the second, write the rhythm. On later hearings, fill in pitches using scale degrees, focusing on large leaps and the final cadence. Melodies often outline chords and use stepwise motion with passing and neighbor tones.

sections.heading: Motive and development on the exam
sections.body: Aural and score-based questions may ask how a motive is developed: repeated, sequenced, inverted, augmented, diminished, or fragmented. Recognizing these devices helps you understand form and composition.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students mislabel suspensions as retardations and forget to measure from the bass.

sections.heading: Worked example: a suspension chain
sections.body: In a 7–6 suspension chain, an upper voice is held over each new bass note to form a seventh, then resolves down to a sixth, creating a descending sequence of dissonance and resolution. Such chains appear often in Baroque music. When analyzing, mark the preparation (consonant), suspension (dissonant, on a strong beat), and resolution (consonant, down by step).

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know passing tone, neighbor tone, suspension, retardation, appoggiatura, escape tone, anticipation, pedal point, motive, sequence, inversion, retrograde, augmentation, diminution, and fragmentation.

sections.heading: Practice routine
sections.body: Analyze one short melody each day by circling chord tones and labeling every non-chord tone. Take a four-bar melodic dictation from a recording or app several times a week, writing the rhythm first and then the pitches. Track which intervals or rhythms cause the most errors and practice those specifically.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: Melodic dictation questions reward accurate rhythms and pitches. Non-chord tones often appear as passing and neighbor tones between chord tones, so recognizing their patterns helps you fill in pitches quickly. When a pitch seems wrong, check whether it creates a reasonable non-chord tone over the implied harmony, and confirm the final notes form a cadence on the tonic or dominant.

keyTakeaways: Classify NCTs by approach and departure.
Escape tone: step in, leap out.
commonMistakes: Mixing up appoggiatura and escape tone.
Labeling suspensions by intervals above the soprano instead of the bass.
Forgetting to identify chord tones first.
examTips: Draw arrows for approach and departure.
Measure suspension intervals from the bass.
guide.cramSheet:
**NCTs:** passing (step–step, same direction) · neighbor (step–step back) · suspension (held → down step) · retardation (held → up step) · appoggiatura (leap–step) · escape (step–leap) · anticipation (early) · pedal (sustained)

**Suspensions:** 4–3 · 7–6 · 9–8 · 2–3 (bass)

**Motive:** sequence · inversion · retrograde · augmentation · diminution · fragmentation

practice.prompt:
Identify each non-chord tone (C major):
(a) Over I, the soprano moves C5–D5–E5 in eighth notes.
(b) Over V, the soprano moves G4–A4–G4.
(c) The alto holds F4 from a IV chord into a I chord (bass C3), then moves to E4.
(d) In V–I, the soprano's C5 sounds on the last eighth of the V chord before I arrives.
(e) Over V, the soprano leaps up to C5 on the downbeat and then steps down to B4.
(f) Over I (bass C3), the soprano holds B4 from a V chord and resolves up to C5.
practice.sampleResponse:
a. D5 is a passing tone between chord tones C and E.
b. A4 is an upper neighbor tone returning to G.
c. F4 is a 4–3 suspension: prepared in IV, dissonant (a 4th above C) over I, resolving down to E (a 3rd).
d. The early C5 is an anticipation of the tonic chord.
e. C5 is an appoggiatura: approached by leap, accented, and resolved by step down to B4, a chord tone of V.
f. B4 is a retardation: held from V and resolving up by step to C5.
